extracted.intended_audience: general readers and stakeholders interested in aviation safety and the Boeing 787 incidents
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing the 2013 Boeing 787 Dreamliner battery incidents, the ensuing fleet groundings, investigations, findings, and remedial actions. It documents technical, regulatory, manufacturing, and investigative issues raised by the incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery manufacturing quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: GS Yuasa of Japan, for battery manufacturing methods that could introduce defects not caught by inspection (as assigned by the NTSB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations and reporting emphasize that manufacturing methods must avoid introducing defects that escape inspection; JTSB later approved Yuasa factory quality control in some respects, while other investigators continued to look for defects in specific batteries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and testing for worst-case battery failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing's engineers, who failed to consider and test for worst-case battery failures (NTSB assignment of blame).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and certification processes should include analysis and testing of worst-case failure modes (e.g., internal short, thermal runaway, cell-to-cell cascade) rather than only nominal operating conditions; investigative coverage cites missing consideration/testing of such scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory certification and testing requirements (FAA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Aviation Administration, that failed to recognize the potential hazard and did not require proper tests as part of its certification process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators must require appropriate tests and assessments during type certification to identify hazards; the article notes FAA approval of a 787 battery in 2007 with nine 'special conditions' and subsequent scrutiny of whether the approval process adequately addressed thermal runaway risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery chemistry safety considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA review focused on lithium-ion batteries that use lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2) as the positive electrode; these electrodes are known for their thermal runaway hazard. Newer, safer types (such as LiFePO4 and LiMn2O4) have since become available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of cell chemistry is a safety-relevant design decision: higher-energy chemistries (e.g., LiCoO2) can provide more energy but bring greater thermal runaway risk, whereas alternatives (LiFePO4, LiMn2O4) provide lower reaction energy in thermal runaway and are considered safer trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery enclosure and containment
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes were required to better contain fires within battery systems; Boeing added an enclosure (reported as 185 lb heavier) to contain thermal events and vented electrolyte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Containment/enclosure design must limit fire propagation and control venting/escape of electrolyte; containment measures may impose weight/operational trade-offs but are necessary to prevent onboard fires from affecting other systems or the airframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electrical compartment fire suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no fire-suppression systems in the electrical compartments holding batteries, only smoke detectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electrical compartments that house batteries should be assessed for whether passive detection (smoke) is sufficient or whether active fire-suppression or improved containment is required to meet safety objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-tolerance expectation for onboard fire
rubrics_metrics.description: NTSB Chairwoman stated that fire must never happen on an aircraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative and regulatory posture treats any onboard fire as unacceptable; design, certification, and operational policies should aim to prevent fires entirely and ensure that battery systems cannot produce uncontained fires during normal operations or foreseeable failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirements to mitigate internal short-circuit effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The NTSB determined the probable cause was an internal short circuit within a cell which led to thermal runaway and cascaded to adjacent cells; the incident resulted from Boeing's failure to incorporate design requirements to mitigate the most severe effects of an internal short circuit within an APU battery cell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design criteria should explicitly require mitigation of worst-case internal short circuits (cell-level failures), including preventing cascade, limiting energy release, and ensuring containment and survivability of adjacent systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding and remedial-action criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA issued an emergency airworthiness directive ordering all U.S.-based airlines to ground their Boeing 787s until yet-to-be-determined modifications were made to the electrical system to reduce the risk of the battery overheating or catching fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may ground fleet types when evidence indicates an unresolved systemic safety hazard; grounding remains appropriate until effective design changes, tests, or procedures demonstrably reduce the identified risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation, oversight, and root-cause identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple investigative bodies (FAA, NTSB, JTSB, congressional hearings) examined causes, oversight, and certification of the 787; the U.S. Senate prepared hearings to look into regulator oversight, safety, and the 2007 FAA certification of the 787.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-incident processes should include transparent multijurisdictional investigation, root-cause analysis, assignment of responsibility (manufacturer, supplier, regulator), and recommendations to prevent recurrence; public and legislative scrutiny can follow to assess oversight adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery monitoring, charging, and electrical system diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations noted that overvoltage was not the cause (voltage did not exceed the 32 V limit) and the charging unit passed tests, but the battery showed signs of short-circuiting and thermal runaway; JTSB reported sudden unexplained voltage drop to near zero and thermal damage to cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Battery systems require robust monitoring and diagnostics able to detect precursors to failure (voltage anomalies, sudden drops, cell damage) and to prevent or isolate faults; charging systems and battery management should be validated against realistic failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplier/component selection and traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents differences between batteries approved by the FAA (made using Kokam cells) and the batteries installed (made by Yuasa), and scrutiny of supplier manufacturing and inspection processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Airframe manufacturers must ensure supplier components meet approved specifications and that changes or alternate suppliers are assessed; traceability, consistent quality assurance, and oversight of supplier factories are essential to maintaining certified design integrity.
